content: Motivational interviewing (MI) is a counseling technique that has been shown to promote positive behavioral changes in the general population. However, its effectiveness in improving outcomes for youth living with HIV remains uncertain. This review aimed to evaluate whether MI can improve specific health outcomes in this population. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple electronic databases, including PubMed, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, EMBASE, LILACS, CINAHL, and PsycINFO, as well as conference proceedings and specialized databases. The search covered studies published between January 1980 and March 2012, without restrictions on language or publication status. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving youth aged 10 to 24 years who were living with HIV. These trials compared MI, either as a standalone intervention or in combination with other interventions, to any other type of intervention. The outcomes of interest included adherence to HIV medication, mortality, quality of life, viral load, CD4-positive T-lymphocyte count, progression to AIDS, retention in care, substance use, and condom use. Studies conducted in any setting were considered. A total of 863 references were initially identified. Two authors independently screened the titles and abstracts, and 28 full-text articles were further assessed for eligibility based on predefined criteria. Ultimately, two trials conducted in the United States, reported across four publications, met the inclusion criteria. These trials enrolled a total of 237 participants and compared MI as a standalone intervention to the standard of care. The quality of the included studies was appraised in duplicate, and data were extracted using a standardized form. No meta-analyses were performed due to the limited number of studies. The two included trials provided moderate-quality evidence suggesting that MI is effective in reducing short-term viral load and the frequency of unprotected sexual acts among youth living with HIV. One of the trials also reported a reduction in alcohol use, but this outcome was not observed in the other trial. Retention in care was assessed in one trial, which found no significant impact of MI on retention rates. Importantly, none of the included trials reported on adherence to HIV medication, mortality, or quality of life. In conclusion, there is moderate-quality evidence from two trials indicating that MI may be effective in reducing short-term viral load and unprotected sexual acts in youth living with HIV. Additionally, there is moderate-quality evidence from one trial suggesting that MI may reduce alcohol use. However, further research is needed to evaluate the impact of MI on other critical outcomes, such as medication adherence, mortality, and quality of life, in this population.
